title: Scheduled tasks
lead: Use cron to run commands repeatedly at specific times. Read the five time fields correctly, define the environment explicitly, and monitor generated output.
objectives: Know the five cron fields in order: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week.
Inspect and edit user jobs with `crontab -l` and `crontab -e`.
Use absolute paths, PATH, and log redirection in cron's limited environment.
Account for distribution differences and the impact of deleting jobs.

sections.title: Cron time and expression format
body: A user crontab line has five time fields and a command: minute (0–59), hour (0–23), day of month (1–31), month (1–12), and day of week (0–7; both 0 and 7 mean Sunday). `*` means every value, `*/15` every 15 intervals, and `1-5` a range.
`0 3 * * *` runs every day at 03:00; `*/15 * * * 1-5` runs every 15 minutes on weekdays. Combining day-of-month and day-of-week can create unexpected matches; verify the schedule you intend.

commands.what: Lists the current user's cron table.
commands.where: When checking whether a job is already scheduled.
commands.why: Helps you avoid adding a duplicate without inspecting existing schedules.

commands.what: Opens the user's cron table in the default editor.
commands.where: When adding or changing a user's scheduled tasks.
commands.why: Manages cron entries without directly editing the system file.

commands.what: Removes the current user's entire crontab.
commands.where: Only when all schedules for that user should deliberately be removed.
commands.why: Deletes every scheduled job; accidental use can cause an outage.

sections.warn: `crontab -r` deletes all jobs for the current user. To remove one job, delete only that line in `crontab -e`; save the output of `crontab -l` first.

sections.title: Cron environment, paths, and logs
body: Cron does not run in an interactive terminal. Profile files may not be loaded, PATH may be limited, and the working directory may not be what you expect. Use absolute paths for executables and files; define `PATH=...` at the top of the crontab if needed.

Redirect standard output and errors to a log file, and manage its growth separately. The time zone depends on system configuration. Test the script manually as the same user first, then verify its permissions and dependencies.

commands.what: Shows the full path of a command.
commands.where: When finding the path of a program for a cron entry.
commands.why: Prevents command-not-found errors caused by cron's limited PATH.

commands.what: Shows the system's local date and time.
commands.where: When investigating schedule or time-zone problems.
commands.why: Lets you compare the system clock that cron uses.

commands.what: Shows the cron service status on Debian/Ubuntu.
commands.where: When scheduled user jobs do not appear to run.
commands.why: Jobs cannot start if the scheduler service is not running.

sections.tip: Use an absolute log path such as `>> /home/student/cron.log 2>&1`; `>` overwrites the file each run, while `>>` appends.

sections.title: Observe and manage jobs safely
body: A user crontab applies only to that user. System-wide cron directories and the root crontab are separate and privileged; do not change their files without authorization. The service is usually `cron` on Debian/Ubuntu and `crond` on RHEL-based systems.

A schedule alone does not prove that a job succeeded: check its log file, service logs, and expected result. A test job that runs every minute creates noise and uses resources; remove it after testing.

commands.what: Displays the user's scheduled jobs again.
commands.where: When verifying an entry after editing.
commands.why: Confirms the entry that was actually saved.

commands.what: Shows the cron service status on RHEL-based systems.
commands.where: When checking the service and distribution differences.
commands.why: Reminds you that the service name varies across distributions.

commands.what: Displays logs for the specified systemd unit.
commands.where: When service logs are written to the systemd journal.
commands.why: Shows scheduler errors and startup records.

sections.danger: Commands in the root crontab run with administrator privileges. Do not run an unfamiliar line; verify its owner and target files. Cron jobs are not suitable for password prompts or interactive input.

t01.text: List the sample schedule files in the simulator with `ls ~/schedule`.
t01.hint: Inspect the real crontab and service in the VM task.

t02.text: Read the sample schedule with `cat ~/schedule/cron.sample`. At what time does the daily backup run?
t02.hint: Read the first five fields, then the command.

t03.text: Show the header with `head -n 1 ~/schedule/cron.sample` and identify the five field names in order.
t03.hint: Minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week.

t04.text: Predict: how often does the sample status check run? Verify with `grep check-status ~/schedule/cron.sample`.

t05.text: Read the incorrect schedule with `cat ~/schedule/wrong-entry.txt`. Find the hour or minute values outside the allowed range.
t05.hint: Hours go up to 23; minutes go up to 59.

t06.text: Remove the file containing the incorrect sample entry: `~/schedule/wrong-entry.txt`.

t07.text: Mini project: write a backup entry that runs daily at 03:00 to `~/schedule/backup-plan.txt`.

t08.text: Challenge: write a job note containing the commands to edit and inspect a schedule to `~/schedule/job-notes.txt`.

t09.text: Ticket: "Cron cannot find the script and its output is lost." Recommend setting PATH, using absolute paths, and redirecting output to a log in the support note.
t09.hint: Use the words `PATH` and `log` in the note.

vm.intro: These tasks inspect the current scheduler; they do not add or remove cron jobs. The service name may differ by distribution.

v01.title: User crontab
v01.text: List the current user's crontab. If no jobs exist, the message is normal; you do not need to add a job.
differs: A `no crontab for ...` message means this user has no entries; you have not done anything wrong.
Only the current user's table is read.

v02.title: Cron service
v02.text: Check the status of your distribution's `cron` or `crond` service.
differs: Debian/Ubuntu usually use `cron`; the RHEL family uses `crond`.
Some WSL/container installations may not run systemd; this is an environment difference.

v03.title: Scheduler logs
v03.text: On systems using the systemd journal, inspect today's cron service records.
differs: The service may be called `crond` on your system; adjust the command.
No log records alone do not prove that a scheduled task failed.

q1.q: What is the order of the five cron time fields?
options: Minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week
q1.explain: A user crontab uses minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week.

options: On the third day of every month
q2.explain: Minute `0`, hour `3`, and all other time fields `*` means daily at 03:00.

q3.q: What is a good first approach if a cron job cannot find `date`?
options: Use the absolute command path or set PATH explicitly
q3.explain: Cron may have a limited PATH; use an absolute command path or set PATH explicitly.

q4.q: What is the safe way to remove one incorrect job?
options: Stop the service and leave it stopped
q4.explain: Removing one line with `crontab -e` leaves the user's other jobs intact.

summary: A user cron entry contains minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, and command.
Use `crontab -e` to edit and `crontab -l` to list and verify.
Absolute paths, an explicit PATH, and log redirection matter in cron's environment.
`crontab -r` deletes all user jobs; edit one line carefully and monitor its output.

glossary.meaning: A table of scheduled jobs for a user or the system.
A time field specifying a minute, hour, day, or month.
The list of directories where the shell searches for commands.
Sending command output to a file or another stream.
